analysis.one_liner: Ties any increase in the federal debt limit to repeal of federal rules, using fast-track procedures.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2019, the bill never left the Senate Homeland Security committee and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make the debt limit, the legal cap on federal borrowing, into a lever for repealing federal regulations. Every time Congress raises the debt limit, Congress would have 60 days to pass legislation cutting the federal cost of regulation by an amount equal to 15% of the increase, using special fast-track procedures. Committees in both chambers would draw up lists of 'major rules' — big rules that affect the economy, costs, or jobs — for repeal, and a repealed rule could not be reissued in the same form without a new law. If Congress failed to act, the debt limit would automatically snap back to current outstanding debt.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses and industries regulated by large federal rules — the bill's repeal mechanism would strip out rules affecting the economy, costs, competition, employment, or investment. Supporters argue that heavy regulation raises prices for consumers and slows the economy; the direct beneficiaries of repealing any specific rule are the entities that were subject to it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries facing major federal rules

how_it_helps.text: Whenever the debt limit is raised, Congress must consider legislation cutting the direct federal cost of regulation over 10 years by at least 15% of the size of the debt limit increase, with an automatic debt-limit penalty if it fails [S2][S3].

Each congressional committee would recommend 'major rules' for repeal — rules with $100 million or more in annual economic effects or major cost increases — and the Budget Committees would combine the lists into a single joint resolution without substantive revision [S2][S3].
A repealed rule could not be reissued in substantially the same form unless Congress specifically authorizes it, making repeals durable [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If a repealed rule had protected health, safety, wages, the environment, or consumers, the cost of losing that protection falls on the people the rule protected. The bill's expedited procedures limit debate and amendments to 10 hours in the Senate, leaving little time to weigh what a repeal takes away.
analysis.who_pays_short: People protected by major federal rules

drawbacks.text: The 'major rules' targeted by the bill are, by definition, the government's most consequential rules — including environmental, consumer, and workplace protections — and fast-track repeal with only 10 hours of Senate debate would leave little room to evaluate what each repeal sacrifices [S2][S3].
If Congress missed the 60-day deadline, the debt limit would automatically reset to current outstanding debt, which could leave the Treasury unable to borrow to pay obligations already incurred [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill bundles unrelated policy — deregulation targets set by the size of a debt increase — into a must-act deadline, and that committees deciding which rules to repeal may weigh industry interests heavily.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's case rests on the claim that federal rules cost more than they deliver, and it does require committees to consider the adverse effects of repealing each rule. But the mechanism is blunt: it converts every debt-limit vote into a mandatory deregulation quota, pushes the largest federal rules toward repeal through fast-track procedures with minimal debate, and could put the government's borrowing authority at risk if Congress does not comply. The gains go to regulated entities; the risks of losing major protections fall on the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Gardner introduced the bill in the Senate on July 31, 2019, with Sen. Mike Lee as its one cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs — and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The bill never received a committee markup or a vote in either chamber before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee, the large federal rules it targeted for repeal — many of which protect consumers, workers, and the environment — remained in place, and regulated industries did not gain the automatic repeal mechanism.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People protected by major federal rules

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Republicans and the bill drew no Democratic cosponsors; it was referred to committee the day it was introduced and never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (finance, energy, manufacturing, and other subjects of major federal rules)
industries.note: The bill creates a standing mechanism to repeal 'major rules' — the government's most consequential rules — automatically triggered by debt-limit increases, and repealed rules cannot be reissued without new legislation. Industries subject to those rules gain by shedding compliance costs; the corresponding protections for consumers, workers, and the environment would be lost.
